title: Write the Money
context: Grade 3, the first working topic of the money chapter that writes an amount. An adult sees an amount being written with a dot, which a paper price tag does well. What is being settled is which part of an amount is the rupees and which is the paise, that the dot is what keeps them apart, that the paise always take two digits, and that an amount said in words and an amount written in figures are one amount. A child who writes 5 paise as one digit after the dot writes 50 paise without knowing it, and a child who reads the number after the dot as a smaller number of rupees will say that 9.05 and 9.5 are the same.

writeup.why: Name the rupees and the paise of a price and see that a hundred paise make a rupee, write an amount with a dot between the rupees and the paise, keep the paise to two digits, and turn an amount from words into figures and from figures into words.
writeup.look: A price tag on a real shop thing with a deep blue Rupees box, a dot and a vermilion Paise box of two cells, a bar of ten blocks beside a Rs 1 coin, a words card, the Words and figures switch, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Write the Money' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many amounts have been written. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A plain shop shelf wall fills the working area. The price tag hangs at x 110, y 214, 470 by 250, from a short string tied to a real thing on the shelf, a ruler, a glue stick, a notebook, a marker or a pencil box. Across the tag run the letters Rs in near-black, the Rupees box in deep blue 150 by 110, a round near-black dot and the Paise box in vermilion, two square cells side by side 70 by 110 each, with the headings Rupees and Paise over the boxes in their own colours. The flat Rs 1 coin stands at x 110, y 520, 120 across, and the bar of ten equal vermilion blocks runs beside it from x 260 to x 620, 60 high, filling one block at a time toward the coin. The words card stands at x 640, y 214, 400 by 130, and says the amount aloud and in writing, such as twelve rupees sixty paise. A green Answer tag at x 640, y 370, 260 by 70, holds the amount the child has typed. In a task the tag sits in a small scene drawn behind it, a classroom shelf, a school fair stall, a stationery shop or a bookstall. The Words and figures switch stands at x 640, y 650, 250 by 60, and the Bar button at x 910, y 650, 130 by 60, each labelled in words. With the switch on, the tag becomes a shop board holding the amount in words, and back. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys, a clear key and a box key that moves the typing between the Rupees box and the Paise box, for typing the rupees and then the paise of an amount into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The whole rupees of an amount are deep blue and the paise are vermilion everywhere, in a column heading, a tag and a label. The value written on one note or coin, and the price of one thing, is amber. How many notes, coins or things there are is sky blue. A total, a change, a converted amount and the answer are green. A note is a plain flat rectangle in its own colour and a coin a plain round disc, each with its value in large near-black type, so a value is read from the number and never from the colour. Anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because an amount is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The tag shows the last amount, with the words card saying it aloud and in writing and the shop board beside it.

writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase a price tag hangs from a ruler on a shop shelf with both boxes filled and unlabelled, and a Rs 1 coin and a bar of ten empty blocks stand under it. On the second the tag hangs from a notebook with two empty boxes and the dot waiting between them. On the third the tag hangs from a pencil box and the Paise box shows two empty cells. On the fourth a shop board holds an amount in words beside an empty tag, and the words card is blank. One thing moves, once: the dot gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on a box is the whole way in.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Money is drawn as plain flat shapes: a note is a rectangle in its own colour and a coin a round disc, each with its value in large near-black type. There is no portrait, no emblem, no serial number and no small print on any note or coin, because a child reads the value from the number. The notes are Rs 500, Rs 200, Rs 100, Rs 50, Rs 20 and Rs 10, and the coins Rs 20, Rs 10, Rs 5, Rs 2 and Rs 1. A note is always longer than it is tall and a coin is always round.

Real everyday things hold the money and the prices: a purse, a money box, a shop shelf with a price tag on each thing, a bill on a counter, a school fair stall. The object is the thing the child counts, pays or reads, and a bare column of figures appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

An amount is always written Rs 25.50: Rs, then the rupees, then a dot, then exactly two digits of paise. Rs 5 and 5 paise is Rs 5.05, and a single digit of paise after the dot is never written. A whole number of rupees may be written without the dot, as Rs 36, or with two zeros, as Rs 36.00.

In a column sum the dots stand in one straight line, rupees to the left of it and paise to the right, with a heading Rupees over one part and Paise over the other. A carry or a borrow of one rupee is written small above the rupees column and its hundred paise above the paise column.
A price is a tag on the thing it belongs to. A bill is a table of the thing, how many, the price of one and the cost, with a rule under the last line and the total below.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a note, a coin, an amount or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a note keeps its own colour, a coin its own metal, a purse its own leather. The whole rupees of an amount are deep blue and the paise are vermilion everywhere, in a column heading, a tag, a label and a typed answer, because the dot between them is the one mark that tells a child which part is which. The value written on one note or coin, and the price of one thing, is amber. How many notes, coins or things there are is sky blue. A total, a change, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Rupees, Paise, Value, How many and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.

voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the paise again. How many cells do they fill?
voice.onNext: A new tag. Which part of the price is the rupees?
voice.opening: A price tag with two boxes and a dot between them, waiting to be filled.
voice.onFinish: You wrote every amount with the dot in the right place.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Fill the boxes with any price you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.

phase_map.concept: Rupees and paise: a hundred paise make a rupee
The dot between the rupees and the paise
Saying and writing an amount in words and in figures

placement.where: After each child has written a few prices on paper price tags by hand and read them aloud to a partner, and before any amount is written on the board. The tool is what makes the paise fill two cells whatever is typed and what turns an amount into words and back, which a paper tag does not do.

answer_key.rule: An amount of money has two parts. The rupees are the whole part and the paise are the small part, and 100 paise make 1 rupee. In figures an amount is written Rs, then the rupees, then a dot, then the paise, and the word paise is not written at the end. Paise always take two digits, so 5 paise is written 05 and the amount is Rs 9.05 and not 9.5. A whole number of rupees may be written with two zeros after the dot, as Rs 8.00, and an amount under one rupee is written with 0 rupees, as Rs 0.07. An amount is said as the rupees and then the paise, so Rs 12.60 is twelve rupees sixty paise.
answer_key.wrong: The tag is shown again with the rupees part in its deep blue box and the paise part in its vermilion box, the dot lit between them and the paise cells counted one, two. The words card says the amount aloud. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The rupees are the whole part of the price: 7.
The paise are the small part of the price: 35.
100 paise make 1 rupee, so the paise of a price are always less than 100.
items.answer: 7 is the rupees and 35 is the paise. 100 paise make 1 rupee.
items.question: The price tag on a ruler says 7 rupees and 35 paise. Which number is the rupees and which is the paise? How many paise make 1 rupee?
items.checkpoint: The paise are a part of a rupee, and 100 paise make 1 rupee.
items.misconception: Thinking 35 is worth more than 7 because 35 is the bigger number.

steps: Write Rs and then the rupees: Rs 16.
Put a dot after the rupees.
Write the paise after the dot, with no word at the end.
items.question: A glue stick costs 16 rupees and 80 paise. Write the price in figures with Rs and a dot.
items.checkpoint: Write Rs, then the rupees, then a dot, then the paise.
items.misconception: Leaving out the dot and writing 1680, or writing the word paise at the end.

steps: 9 has only one digit, so write a 0 in front of it: 09.
items.question: A sticker costs 4 rupees and 9 paise. Write the price in figures.
items.checkpoint: Paise take two digits, so 9 paise is written 09.
items.misconception: Writing 4.9, which means 4 rupees and 90 paise.

steps: Ten paise is 10, and it already has two digits.
Put a dot between them: Rs 48 and 10 paise is Rs 48.10.
items.question: A shop board says forty-eight rupees ten paise. Write the amount in figures.
items.checkpoint: Say the rupees first, then the paise, and write a dot between them.
items.misconception: Writing 48.1 and dropping the 0 of the ten paise.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: The price tag on a pencil box says 23 rupees and 50 paise. Which number is the rupees? Which number is the paise?
items.final_answer: 23 is the rupees and 50 is the paise

items.question: A marker costs 11 rupees and 40 paise. Write the price in figures with Rs and a dot.
items.final_answer: Rs 11.40, because Rs 11 and 40 paise is Rs 11.40

items.question: A candy costs 2 rupees and 7 paise. Write the price in figures.
A board in a stationery shop says thirty rupees sixty paise. Write the amount in figures.
A child writes 9 rupees and 20 paise as 920. What is missing? Write the price correctly.
items.final_answer: The dot is missing. The price is Rs 9.20, because Rs 9 and 20 paise is Rs 9.20

items.question: At the school fair a child writes 13 rupees and 6 paise as 13.6. What is wrong? Write the price correctly.
items.final_answer: The paise must take two digits. 6 paise is written 06, so the price is Rs 13.06

items.question: A small eraser costs only 85 paise. Starting with Rs, write its price in figures. How many rupees are there?
items.final_answer: Rs 0.85, because 85 paise is Rs 0.85. There are 0 rupees

items.question: A tag on a bookstall shelf says Rs 36.00. How many paise are in the price? Write the same price with no dot.
items.final_answer: There are no paise. The price is Rs 36, because Rs 36.00 is Rs 36

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: holds the rupees of the amount and takes the typed digits
holds the paise in two cells and slides a 0 in front of a single digit
moves the typing between the Rupees box and the Paise box
turns the tag into a shop board that holds the amount in words, and back
fills ten blocks toward the Rs 1 coin, a hundred paise in all
says the amount aloud and in writing
types the digits of the rupees and of the paise

teaching_notes: Give each child a paper price tag with two boxes and a dot drawn on it before the tool opens, and ask them to write a few prices for classroom things and read them aloud. Always ask which part is the rupees and which is the paise before a digit is typed, and say each amount aloud as the rupees and then the paise, as in twelve rupees sixty paise. Wait for a child to say that the paise take two digits, rather than saying it for them. If a child writes a single digit of paise, ask how many digits paise take and how many cells the paise box has. Use fresh amounts: the printed amounts are the child's to write.
generation_prompt: Build an amount-writing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A price tag hangs from a short string on a real thing on a shop shelf at the left of the working area. Across the tag run the letters Rs in near-black, a deep blue Rupees box, a round near-black dot and a vermilion Paise box of two square cells, with the headings Rupees and Paise over the boxes. A single digit typed into the Paise box makes a 0 slide into the cell in front of it. A flat Rs 1 coin and a bar of ten equal vermilion blocks stand under the tag, and the bar fills one block at a time toward the coin. A words card says the amount aloud and in writing. A Words and figures switch turns the tag into a shop board that holds the amount in words and back. A green Answer tag holds the amount the child has typed. Each task sits in a small scene, a classroom shelf, a school fair stall, a stationery shop or a bookstall. The number pad types the digits and a box key moves the typing between the two boxes. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of amounts written. A note is a plain flat rectangle and a coin a plain round disc, each with only its value on it, and the rupee sign is never drawn: an amount is written Rs 25.50. No people, hands or faces. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Fill the boxes of the price tag. Put the dot between the rupees and the paise. Give the paise two digits. Say each amount aloud.
